result.summary: The hymn praises Ares with a long list of titles as a strong, bronze-armed warrior god and defender of Olympus. The speaker then prays that Ares will give him courage against cowardice, restrain his own violent anger, and let him live in peace.

scenes.title: Hymn and prayer to Ares
scenes.summary: The speaker praises Ares by his many titles and then asks him to strengthen his courage, calm his fury and keep him in peace.
scenes.stakes: The speaker risks being ruled by cowardice or by his own violent fury, and hopes to live in peace.

notable_quotes.reason: The hymn turns from war to a prayer for peace, which is unusual for a hymn to a war god.

analysis.text: The hymn praises Ares as a protector and then asks him to restrain the speaker's own rage. It treats the war god's strength as something to be controlled and turned toward peace and justice.
The mention of the seven planets in their courses and the firmaments reflects later astronomical ideas. This suggests the hymn was composed late and shows the influence of Hellenistic astrology.

fun_facts.text: Unlike most Homeric Hymns, this one has no myth in it. It is a string of epithets followed by a prayer, and some scholars think it was composed late.

language_notes.text: "Doughty" means brave and stout-hearted; an old-fashioned epithet for a warrior.
"Ally of Themis" links Ares to Themis, the goddess of right order and law, presenting him as a defender of justice.
The "sevenfold courses" of the planets reflect later astronomical ideas of seven wandering bodies, Ares being identified with the planet Mars.
"Blood-curdling" describes strife that chills the blood with horror.
"Give you me" is an archaic imperative: "you, give me" boldness.

context_notes.text: Ares is the Greek god of war, son of Jove and Juno. This hymn is unusual in praising him as a protector and asking for peace.
Victory (Nike) was a goddess; calling Ares her father makes him the source of success in battle.

literary_notes.text: A long string of titles such as "Saviour of cities" and "golden-helmed" characterizes Ares in the traditional hymnic style of invocation.
The speaker directly addresses the god, opening the hymn as a formal invocation before the request.
Strength is pictured as a "kindly ray" shed from above, like light from the heavens, and cowardice is something to drive from the head.
The peaceful laws are set against strife, hatred and death's fiends, reversing the war-god's usual role in the prayer's turn.
